newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico worried, indignant on possible drug censure.
newsitem.headline: Mexico worried, indignant on possible drug censure.

text.p: As the Clinton administration decides whether to publicly censure Mexico's record in the drug war, Mexican officials warned on Tuesday that an adverse U.S. decision could trigger an anti-American backlash.
The U.S. government is likely to announce by the end of the week its annual assessment of how countries around the world are performing in the fight against narcotics.

Political pressure is mounting on President Bill Clinton to take a hard line against Mexico this year because of the firing last week of its top anti-drug official, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, on suspicion of collaborating with drug lords.

No one seriously expects Mexico to be "decertified" -- the harshest option that implies economic sanctions -- but a slap on the wrist via a conditional certification with a national security waiver is a possibility.

That has angered Mexican government officials, business leaders and citizens. They say Americans are unjustly attacking their valiant anti-narcotics efforts, while ignoring the fact that the United States is the main market for the illegal drugs smuggled through Mexico.

Carlos Gutierrez, president of the industry association Canacintra, said: "This is now not (just) an attack on the government or on some person but I think this is an attack on Mexico. This is something which we totally reject ... the name of Mexico should under no circumstances be put on trial."
Fellow business leader Carlos Abascal said the drug certification process was "an abuse of international law" and an intrusion in internal affairs.
President Ernesto Zedillo did not refer explicitly to the certification debate in a speech on Tuesday.
But his reference to "the absurd pretense that Mexico is inevitably a country of crime and corruption" was taken here as a veiled warning to critics of his efforts against the drug cartels.

Mexican government officials said they had been annoyed by some of the foreign reaction to the dismissal of the general. "The reaction to this (the general's firing) was terrible," one senior official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

"President (Ernesto) Zedillo showed leadership and took the right decision ... he wanted to go all the way on this and he will go all the way in future. Some of the Americans understand this ... but others don't."
Officials admitted an "embarrassing" failure of army intelligence, which had given Gen. Gutierrez a clean bill of health before he took up his highly sensitive post last December.
"But remember that this was also a failure of U.S. intelligence," one official said. "They also had no (adverse) information about him ... they really liked him."

Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria warned on Monday that any U.S. censure of Mexico could lead to a "fracture" in the "excellent" relations between the two North American Free Trade Agreement partners.

Government officials expressed their concern that any failure to grant full certification would lead to an outburst of anti-American sentiment, which might endanger the success of Clinton's first visit to Mexico in April.
"I am worried about the anti-American feeling which is being developed among different sectors, in the Church, on the left and on the right," one official said.
